one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

Aone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

pone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

 one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

.one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

tone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

rone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

Done). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

tone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

-one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

tone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

 one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

bone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

oone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

gone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

oone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

 one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

 one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

eone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

oone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

eone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

tone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

hone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

,one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

-one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

lone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

tone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

 one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

cone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

Fone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

*one). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

oone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

sone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

eone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

bone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

done). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

aone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

tone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.

Frames go to the compositor in **GPU memory as NV12**, the YUV format decoders put out:
ffmpeg only crops (no conversion to RGB, no scaling unless the video is far bigger than
the screen), and the compositor converts and scales on the GPU as it draws, without
copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

copying each frame up to it. The GPU buffers come from GBM (`libgbm1`, loaded when a video
first plays). Where that isn't possible (no GPU driver with GBM, a compositor that doesn't
take NV12 buffers), ffmpeg scales and converts to RGB and frames go through shared memory,
which takes about 40% more CPU. `herowallpaper --status` says which way videos play.
`HEROWALLPAPER_NO_GPU=1` forces shared memory; `HEROWALLPAPER_DEBUG=1` prints the decoder
and ffmpeg filter used.

eone). Frames are only read while the compositor draws the wallpaper, so ffmpeg waits
whenever windows cover it.

**Videos bigger than the screen** (a 4K one on a laptop) or faster than 60 frames a second
get a copy fitted to the screen, made once in the background at the lowest priority (the
first frame shows as a still meanwhile) and kept in `~/.cache/herowallpaper` (the 6 used
last). Decoding a 4K 60 fps video takes about 9 times the CPU of its 1366×768 copy:
measured 23 s of CPU for 5 s of a 4K60 clip (more than 4 cores, so it can't keep up),
2.7 s for its copy.

Decoding: the chip's own video decoder first where it has one ARM-style (V4L2, FFmpeg's
`h264_v4l2m2m` and the like), then whatever `-hwaccel auto` finds (VA-API...), then the
CPU; each is kept if it gives a first frame.
